title: Circumference of a Circle, and Miles and Kilometres
summary: Discover π as circumference ÷ diameter, use C = πd and C = 2πr (forwards and backwards), and convert between miles and kilometres with 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km and 1 km ≈ 5/8 mile.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand that **π (pi)** is the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter (circumference ÷ diameter). Know and use the formula for the **circumference** of a circle: C = πd (or C = 2πr). (8Gg.02)
Know that distances can be measured in **miles** or **kilometres**: 1 mile is about 1.6 km, and 1 km is about 5/8 of a mile. Use these facts to convert. (8Gg.03)

blocks.text: 1. Key words

items: centre
المركز — the point in the middle, the same distance from every point on the circle
radius (r)
نصف القطر — from the centre to the circle
diameter (d)
القطر — across the circle through the centre; d = 2r
circumference (C)
محيط الدائرة — the distance all the way round a circle
π (pi)
باي (ط) — circumference ÷ diameter, about 3.14
ratio
نسبة — how many times bigger one quantity is than another
semicircle
نصف دائرة — half of a circle, cut along a diameter
perimeter
المحيط — the total distance round the edge of any shape
mile / kilometre (km)
ميل / كيلومتر — units of long distance
approximately (≈)
تقريبًا — nearly equal

blocks.text: 2. What is π?
Take any circle: a coin, a cup, a plate, a bicycle wheel. Measure its circumference (wrap a string round it) and its diameter. Then work out **circumference ÷ diameter**.

For **every** circle, big or small, C ÷ d gives the same number, just over 3. (The small differences in the table come from measuring errors.) This number is called **π** (the Greek letter pi). Its decimal digits never end and never repeat: π = 3.14159… We usually use **π ≈ 3.14** or the **π key** on a calculator.

blocks.title: The formulae
items: **π = C ÷ d** (π is the ratio of circumference to diameter).
So **C = π × d**, usually written **C = πd**.
Because d = 2r, also **C = 2 × π × r = 2πr**.
To find the diameter from the circumference: **d = C ÷ π**. Then r = d ÷ 2.

blocks.title: يعني إيه π؟
blocks.text: لو قسمت محيط أي دائرة على قطرها هيطلع لك نفس الرقم دايمًا، تقريبًا 3.14 — ده اسمه π. يعني المحيط أطول من القطر حوالي 3 مرات وشوية. القانون: المحيط = π × القطر (C = πd)، ولو معاك نصف القطر: المحيط = 2 × π × نصف القطر. وخلي بالك: لو السؤال إداك نصف القطر، اضربه في 2 الأول.
3. Finding the circumference, step by step

items: Read the question: is the length a **radius** or a **diameter**? If it is a radius, double it (or use C = 2πr).
Write the formula: C = πd.
Substitute: for example C = π × 12.
Calculate. With a calculator use the π key. Without a calculator use the value the question gives (often 3.14).
Round as the question asks (for example to 1 decimal place) and write the **unit** (cm, m…). Circumference is a length, so the unit is NOT squared.
Check: the answer should be a bit more than 3 × the diameter.

blocks.text: **Perimeter of a semicircle** = half the circumference + the diameter (the straight edge). Many students forget the straight edge.
4. Miles and kilometres

Distances between towns are measured in **kilometres** in most countries (Egypt uses km), but in some countries, such as the UK and the USA, road signs and speeds use **miles**. A mile is longer than a kilometre.

blocks.title: The facts to learn (8Gg.03)
items: **1 mile ≈ 1.6 km** → miles to km: **multiply by 1.6** (or × 8 ÷ 5).
**1 km ≈ 5/8 of a mile** → km to miles: **multiply by 5/8** (divide by 8, then multiply by 5).
Easy pair to remember: **5 miles ≈ 8 km**.
Both facts are approximate (a mile is really a little more than 1.6 km), so use ≈ and 'about'.

blocks.text: **Check your answer makes sense:** the number of **kilometres is always bigger** than the number of miles for the same distance (because a kilometre is the shorter unit, you need more of them).

Because miles and kilometres are in **direct proportion**, a conversion graph is a straight line through (0, 0). To use it, go up from the value on one axis to the line, then across to the other axis.

blocks.title: تحويل الميل والكيلومتر
items: الميل أطول من الكيلومتر: 1 ميل ≈ 1.6 كم. من ميل لكيلو: اضرب في 1.6.
من كيلو لميل: اضرب في 5/8 (اقسم على 8 واضرب في 5).
احفظ: 5 ميل ≈ 8 كم. وعدد الكيلومترات دايمًا أكبر من عدد الأميال لنفس المسافة.

blocks.text: 5. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** [2 marks] (calculator)
A circular clock face has diameter **12 cm**. Calculate its circumference. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

items: C = πd = π × 12
= 37.699… (calculator)
**Answer: 37.7 cm** (1 mark for π × 12 seen, 1 mark for 37.7).
Check: 3 × 12 = 36, and 37.7 is a bit more. ✓

blocks.text:
**Worked example 2** [2 marks] (calculator)
A circular flower bed has **radius 4.5 m**. Calculate its circumference to 1 decimal place.

items: Radius given, so d = 2 × 4.5 = 9 m (or use C = 2πr).
**Answer: 28.3 m**.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** π × 4.5 = 14.1 m. That uses the radius as if it were the diameter, giving only half the circumference.

**Worked example 3** [1 mark] (no calculator)
Use π = 3.14 to work out the circumference of a circle with diameter **10 cm**.
C = 3.14 × 10 = **31.4 cm**. (Multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place to the left.)

**Worked example 4** [2 marks] (calculator)
The circumference of a round tray is **50 cm**. Work out its diameter, correct to 1 decimal place.

items: C = πd, so d = C ÷ π.
**Answer: 15.9 cm.** (If the question asks for the radius: 15.915… ÷ 2 = 7.96 → 8.0 cm.)

blocks.text:
**Worked example 5** [3 marks] (calculator)
The diagram shows a semicircle with diameter 8 cm. Calculate its perimeter to 1 decimal place.

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 160" width="300" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><path d="M50 130A100 100 0 0 1 250 130Z" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2.2"/><text x="150" y="152" text-anchor="middle">8 cm</text><circle cx="150" cy="130" r="3" fill="#0f1b33"/><text x="150" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">NOT TO SCALE</text></svg>
blocks.caption: A semicircle with diameter 8 cm.

items: Full circumference = π × 8 = 25.132…
Curved part = half of that = 12.566…
Perimeter = curved part + straight diameter = 12.566… + 8 = 20.566…
**Answer: 20.6 cm.** (1 mark for π × 8 ÷ 2, 1 mark for adding 8, 1 mark for 20.6.)

blocks.text:
**Worked example 6** [3 marks] (calculator)
A bicycle wheel has diameter 70 cm. How far does the bicycle travel when the wheel turns 100 times? Give your answer in metres, to the nearest metre.

items: One turn moves the bicycle one circumference: π × 70 = 219.91… cm.
**Answer: 220 m.**

blocks.text:
**Worked example 7** [1 mark]
A road sign in England says 'London 45 miles'. About how many kilometres is this?
45 × 1.6 = 45 + (45 × 0.6) = 45 + 27 = **72 km**.

**Worked example 8** [2 marks]
A journey is **120 km**. Use 1 km ≈ 5/8 mile to change this to miles.
120 ÷ 8 = 15, then 15 × 5 = **75 miles**. Check: 75 is smaller than 120 ✓ (miles are fewer).

**Worked example 9** [2 marks]
Route A is 50 miles long. Route B is 85 km long. Which route is shorter, and by how many kilometres?
Change to the same unit: 50 miles ≈ 50 × 1.6 = 80 km. 80 km < 85 km, so **Route A is shorter, by about 5 km**.
**Common mistake:** comparing 50 with 85 directly. You must change both distances to the same unit first.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Using the radius in C = πd. If you are given r, double it first, or use C = 2πr.
Mixing up circumference and area. Circumference is a length (cm), not cm².
Forgetting the straight edge (the diameter) when finding the perimeter of a semicircle.
Rounding too early. Keep the full calculator value until the last step, then round.
Converting the wrong way: dividing by 1.6 to change miles to km. Ask yourself: should the number get bigger or smaller?
Writing 1 km = 1.6 miles. It is 1 **mile** ≈ 1.6 km.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Calculate the circumference… Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place." Show the substitution (π × 12) for the method mark.
Paper 1 (no calculator) gives you a value such as π = 3.14, or asks you to estimate with π ≈ 3. Paper 2 (calculator): use the π key.
Reverse questions: the circumference is given, find the diameter or radius (divide by π).
Real contexts: wheels turning, running tracks, fences round circular gardens, semicircular windows.
"Draw a ring around" the best estimate of a distance in miles, or complete a conversion table.
Conversion graphs: read across and up carefully; use the grid squares to find the scale first.
"Explain" questions: 'π is circumference ÷ diameter, so…' and 'kilometres are shorter than miles, so the number is bigger'.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Circumference, miles and kilometres — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. A calculator is allowed unless the question gives you a value of π to use.

questions.q: Which of these is the definition of π?
questions.e: π is the ratio of the circumference to the diameter: π = C ÷ d ≈ 3.14. (Circumference ÷ radius would be 2π ≈ 6.28; radius × 2 is the diameter.)

questions.q: A circle has diameter 9 cm. Calculate its circumference. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
A circle has radius 5 cm. Which calculation gives its circumference?
questions.e: C = 2πr = 2 × π × 5 (= π × 10 = 31.4 cm). π × 5 uses the radius as the diameter; π × 5 × 5 is the area.

questions.q: Use π = 3.14 to work out the circumference of a circle with diameter 20 cm. (No calculator.)
The circumference of a circular mirror is 88 cm. Calculate its diameter, correct to 1 decimal place.

questions.p: The top of a window is a semicircle with diameter 14 cm.
questions.q: Calculate the perimeter of the semicircle, correct to 1 decimal place.
questions.e: Curved part = π × 14 ÷ 2 = 21.991… cm. Perimeter = 21.991… + 14 (the straight diameter) = 35.991… = 36.0 cm (1 d.p.).

questions.q: A wheel has radius 30 cm. It turns 50 times. How far does it travel? Give your answer in metres, to the nearest metre.
Use 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km. Change 35 miles to kilometres.
Use 1 km ≈ 5/8 mile. Change 200 km to miles.
questions.e: 200 ÷ 8 = 25, then 25 × 5 = 125 miles. Check: fewer miles than km ✓.

questions.q: Which distance is the **longest**? (Use 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km.)
questions.e: Change all to km: 60 km; 40 miles ≈ 64 km; 62 000 m = 62 km; 38 miles ≈ 60.8 km. The longest is 40 miles.

questions.q: Hassan measures a round plate. He writes: 'diameter = 24 cm, circumference = 85 cm'. Explain how you know he has made a mistake.
questions.ms: 1 mark: compares C ÷ d with π, e.g. 85 ÷ 24 ≈ 3.5, which is not about 3.14 (accept 'too big'). 1 mark: the circumference should be about π × 24 ≈ 75 cm (accept 75–76 cm, or 3 × 24 = 72 as an estimate showing 85 is too big).
questions.e: For every circle, circumference ÷ diameter = π ≈ 3.14. Here 85 ÷ 24 ≈ 3.54, which is too big. The circumference should be π × 24 ≈ 75.4 cm, so one of his measurements is wrong.

questions.q: A circular pond has circumference 47.1 m. Use π = 3.14 to find its **radius**.
A speed limit in the UK is 50 miles per hour. About how many kilometres per hour is this?
questions.e: 50 miles ≈ 50 × 1.6 = 80 km, so 50 miles per hour ≈ 80 km per hour. (31 km/h comes from multiplying by 5/8, which is the wrong way.)

questions.q: Use the graph to change 25 miles to kilometres.
questions.e: Go up from 25 on the miles axis to the line, then across to the km axis: 40 km. Check: 25 × 1.6 = 40 ✓.

blocks.title: Remember
items: π = circumference ÷ diameter ≈ 3.14, the same for every circle.
C = πd = 2πr. If you know C, then d = C ÷ π.
Semicircle perimeter = half of πd + the diameter.
1 mile ≈ 1.6 km and 1 km ≈ 5/8 mile (5 miles ≈ 8 km).
Miles → km: × 1.6 (number gets bigger). km → miles: ÷ 8 × 5 (number gets smaller).
